tip: After a superlative like 'il miglior vino', the relative clause usually takes the subjunctive: 'abbia bevuto'.
Adverbs like 'sempre' usually go between the helper and the participle: 'ha sempre incuriosito', not after it.
'Prima che' always takes the subjunctive: 'torni' is the subjunctive of 'tornare'.
'Bisognava che' needs the subjunctive: 'trovassi' is the imperfect subjunctive of 'trovare'.
'Dove' works as a relative for places, standing in for 'in cui': 'la spiaggia dove andiamo'.
Reflexive verbs form compound tenses with 'essere', and the participle agrees: 'si era addormentata' (feminine).
Before the direct object 'la', the indirect pronoun 'ti' becomes 'te': 'te la direi' (I'd tell it to you).
'Per cui' means 'why' or 'for which' after a noun: 'il motivo per cui' (the reason why).
'Il quale' and its forms can replace 'cui' after a preposition: 'nella quale' = 'in cui' (in which).
Unreal if: 'se' plus the imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional: 'se lavorassi..., avrei' (if I worked, I'd have).
'Essere d'accordo' takes 'su' for the thing agreed on, so the relative is 'su cui' (on which).
'Cui' placed between an article and a noun means 'whose': 'sulla cui cima' (on whose top).
'Stare' plus the gerund makes the -ing present: 'sto imparando' (am learning).
'Chi' means 'whoever' or 'he who' and always takes a singular verb: 'chi lavora' (whoever works).
Italian stacks negatives: 'non ... mai' is literally not ... never, yet 'non avevano mai assaggiato' just means had never tasted.
With reciprocal 'si' and 'essere', the past participle agrees with the subject: 'incontrati' ends in -i for a masculine or mixed group.
'Come se' (as if) always takes the subjunctive: 'come se niente fosse successo', never 'è successo'.
The future perfect can express a guess about the past: 'avrà dimenticato' means 'he must have forgotten', not a real future.
'Magari' plus the imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish: 'magari il tempo passasse', if only time passed.
The 'had done' tense = the imperfect of 'avere' or 'essere' plus the participle: 'avevano costruito', they had built.
For real, likely conditions, 'se' takes the present indicative: 'se trovi', not a subjunctive. Save the subjunctive for hypotheticals.
Unreal present 'if': 'se' plus the imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional: 'se sapessi guidare, affitterei'.
'Pure' after a command softens it to 'go ahead, feel free': 'chiedi pure', just ask.
'Dimenticarsi' takes 'di' before the thing forgotten; 'di' contracts with the article here: 'del suo compleanno'.
'Volere che' forces the subjunctive: 'volevano che partissimo', never 'volevano che partivamo'.
A past main verb like 'volevo' pulls the following subjunctive into the past, so it is 'venissi', not 'venga': 'volevo che tu venissi'.
'Stesso' after a time word means 'this very': 'domani stesso', tomorrow itself, no later.
The dell' in 'dell'acqua' is 'di' plus the article, the partitive for 'some': 'c'è dell'acqua', there's some water.
The future perfect marks an action finished before a future point: 'avrò consegnato', I will have handed it in.
Object pronouns attach to the end of an infinitive, which drops its final -e: 'ringraziare' plus 'ti' becomes 'ringraziarti', to thank you.
